program: Culturally specific survivor safety, counseling and practical support
priceScope: Initial $265.40M annual diagnostic retained for comparison; current limited signed reference nonpositive. Complete portfolio and marginal gift EV unknown.

what: Daya supports South Asian survivors of domestic and sexual violence in the Houston region.
It combines confidential crisis support, licensed counseling, housing assistance and economic empowerment.
Culturally specific advocacy and legal referrals help survivors pursue safety and practical stability.
strengths: Culturally specific advocacy addresses language and access barriers.
Freshly checked program counts support distinct counseling, housing and work-resource mechanisms.
Comparative primary evidence informs integrated safety scenarios without treating services as causal outcomes.
reservations: Service groups overlap and completed dose, households and local causal effects remain unobserved.
Current costs and newer outputs differ in vintage; monetary assistance is not net new income.
The limited modeled reference is nonpositive under retained burden priors; broader safety and whole portfolio remain uncertain.

sections.what: Daya supports South Asian survivors of domestic and sexual violence in the Houston region. It combines confidential crisis support, licensed counseling, housing assistance and economic empowerment. Culturally specific advocacy and legal referrals help survivors pursue safety and practical stability.
sections.monitoring: Freshly fetched and visually checked 2025 official report: 683 clients, 564 crisis/safety,75 counseling,75 housing,109 economic users; these overlap and are not distinct households or completed effective doses. County shares 63% Harris+20% Fort Bend+4% Brazoria/Galveston/Montgomery give .87 local share once; other Texas/out-of-state excluded. Assistance spending includes $110,000 housing, $28,000 legal, $12,000 transport and $47,000 essentials, not measured causal net resources. Request an overlap/dose ledger, local unique households, housing retention, symptom/utility follow-up, after-tax earnings and benefits lost, alternative services, exposure cost and retaliation/privacy outcomes.
sections.qualitative: The original 2023 JAMA DVHF study compared 219 housing-first and 125 usual-service participants in a weighted nonrandom analytic cohort of 344 over two years. Housing, safety and mental-health advantages support integrated mechanisms, but confounding, Washington setting and few Asian participants limit transfer. Symptom scales are not measured QALYs or Daya income. PATH's original 2018 randomized trial compared specialist psychological advocacy with usual advocacy; improved distress/depression at 12 months but no demonstrated further-abuse difference, with 64% retention. Dose 8 sessions plus 2 follow-ups is not Daya's unspecified counseling dose. These results motivate overlap-bounded counseling/housing and broad-safety scenarios, not assigning full DVHF to all 683 or summing depression, anxiety and housing utility. Current services include licensed therapy, practical assistance, job-search support and legal referral, not staff attorneys. Existing victim agencies, public aid, family and employer support remain alternatives. Culturally appropriate access may add value without proving universal response.
sections.cost: Initial $265.40 M is retained as the complete historical health-and-income diagnostic: health +0.076447 and income −0.003090. Burden-only correction gives combined −0.852807; additional native-program restriction gives current health −0.077592, income −1.134818, total −1.212410, so no finite positive current price. This is not a measured harm finding about Daya or its whole portfolio. Full FY 2024 annual $1,946,855 expense is matched conditionally to FY 2025 service outputs; unmodeled legal, safety, other housing and prevention benefits remain unknown, not zero. Clinical envelope 75 assumes maximum overlap of 75 counseling/75 housing; range 75–150 is tested, replacing rather than adding two utility streams. Retained .8 household mapping, .35 additionality, .35 clinical response, .05 utility for .5 year are judgments, not trial coefficients. Broader 564 safety/crisis utility replaces that stream; low-response and high-intensity hypotheses bound possibilities but none establish that every brief-contact user got a housing-first dose. Central gain groups are bounded to 109 economic and 75 housing users with 75 assumed overlap; .8*.35*.25 resource-response scale gives 5.25 joint resource-success and 2.38 work-only proxies, not successes on all 683. Net work $300 and assistance $500 after alternative aid, taxes and benefit withdrawals remain hypotheses; positive overlap .5 before joint log, then full $100 participation/safety/opportunity costs. Other exposed household proxies retain negative costs; clinical harm .0005 applies all 546.4 exposures even when b=0. These unmeasured burdens are decisive; weighted burden (109 intensive proxies at$100, remaining at$10) still has nonpositive combined reference. The $100 uniform prior is not an observed average for brief helpline users. Distinct transfer counterparties and provider losses are localized once, with full losses, no overlap haircut. No grants' face value, gross salary or ordinary survivor earnings is counted as new social income. Payer zero is unknown-neutral, not measured zero. No-exposure/no-gift, financial-only, clinical-null, adverse, alternative, finite duration, overlap and volunteer-cost regimes are explicit. Broad high-dose positive sensitivity remains a hypothesis rather than a favorable central chosen to rescue price. Work resources are after childcare, commute, taxes and benefit withdrawal; the separately modeled participation cost must exclude any work expense already deducted. The income model uses one welfare-equivalent adult per household at $20,000 baseline, not every family member.
sections.funding: FY 2024 $1,928,451 tax expenses plus $18,404 netted direct event cost gives $1,946,855. FY 2023 $1,694,184 plus $18,861 gives $1,713,045; FY 2022 $1,417,570 plus $16,537 gives $1,434,107. Schedule D reconciles expense totals without a populated additional donated-resource adjustment. This is not evidence that volunteer resources cost zero. Newer FY 2025 outputs versus FY 2024 cost are a conditional scope mismatch. Reserves do not demonstrate an expansion bottleneck. Fresh root verification of the FY 2024 original confirms the accepted full-cost numerator. Fresh 2025 output PDF has no matching audited FY 2025 expense or current marginal-gift bottleneck. Recipient assistance expense is already in C; separate payer-incidence scenarios represent displaced public/private alternatives, not adding the same recipient grant expense twice.

model.costScope: Full annual recipient expense versus overlap-bounded counseling/housing and restricted economic channels; other portfolio and next gift unknown
model.geographicAttribution: Reported 2025 county shares imply .87 Houston MSA; applied once
model.formula: Exposed=N*unique; union=exposed*b; clinical=(clinicalN*unique*b*clinicalResponse*q*finite discounted T − full exposed*harm)*g. Work/assistance success partitions=program counts*unique*b*success with intersection once. One joint log per disjoint household partition of overlap-adjusted positive resources minus full costs; all other exposure retains costs. Distinct transfer payer loss local once. Price=10*C/(health+signed income) only if positive.
model.counterfactual: Other victim services, public benefits, legal aid, family support and employment alternatives retained
model.attribution: Annual incremental recipient response is distinct from cohort deduplication and geographic share; no claim of whole annual portfolio or marginal donation causal effect.
model.uncertainty: Primary comparative evidence supports mechanisms, not local utility or net income coefficients. Household/program intersection and full exposure burdens unmeasured; no finite positive current conditional reference. Unmodeled channels and marginal-gift EV remain unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional integrated safety/mental-health, stable housing and net disposable work/assistance resources; output counts not causal outcomes.
